ut.description: On-site ultrasonic testing in San Antonio, TX: wall thickness surveys on tanks, vessels and piping plus UT weld examination to code. Ask for a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in San Antonio, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to plants, fabrication shops, hangars and rail-served industrial sites in San Antonio for two jobs: ultrasonic thickness testing on tanks, pressure vessels, piping and structural steel, and ultrasonic weld inspection with angle-beam shear-wave probes. Send us the component list, the governing code and the access conditions and we will scope the examination and quote it. Use the quote request form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in San Antonio

San Antonio is a manufacturing, military and logistics city rather than a single-industry refining town, and that mix shapes the UT work. The metro area ranks among the larger manufacturing markets in Texas, with automotive assembly (a full-size truck plant opened south of downtown in 2006 and pulled a ring of stamping, seating and interior suppliers around it), aerospace repair and overhaul, food processing, and energy-related fabrication. Each of these produces steel that wears out in a recognizable way.

At Port San Antonio, the former Kelly Air Force Base, roughly 1,900 acres hold hangars, an industrial airfield, warehousing and an on-site railport served by Union Pacific and BNSF. Hangar structures, crane rails, ground-support equipment, rail spurs, fuel and utility piping and the loading structures at a railport all need periodic wall thickness checks and weld verification. Food and beverage plants add stainless process piping, steam headers and compressed-air receivers, where the question is usually remaining wall on carbon-steel utility lines and weld quality on repairs.

The power side matters too. A large municipal utility serves the city, and gas-fired generation, boiler feedwater and steam piping, and cooling-water lines are classic thickness-survey subjects. South of the city the Eagle Ford play feeds gathering lines, compressor stations, separators and storage tanks, and San Antonio is where many of the fabrication, hauling and service companies for that work operate. Pressure vessels on skids, flare knockout drums and tank shells are routine UT subjects for those operators when they are not in a refinery.

Ultrasonic thickness testing on corroded steel

A thickness survey answers one question: how much wall is left at each point, and how fast is it going? A technician sets up a dual-element probe, which separates transmit and receive crystals so the sound path works on rough, corroded or pitted outer surfaces, and calibrates it on a step block made of the same material as the component. On carbon steel the velocity is close to a standard value, but a step block at the actual thickness range removes the guesswork and shows zero-offset errors before they enter the data.

Readings are taken on a marked grid, usually at the condition monitoring locations (CMLs) set by the owner's inspection plan. The technician watches the A-scan, not only the digital readout, because a gauge that locks onto a laminar indication or doubles on a thin wall will report a plausible but wrong number. Where a surface is scaled, we grind to bright metal over a small footprint, apply couplant and record whether the reading came from clean metal or a prepared spot. For hot lines, high-temperature probes and couplant are used and the reading is corrected for temperature using the procedure's correction factors.

Method background sits in ASME Section V, Article 5 for ultrasonic examination of materials, ASTM E797 for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, and our own guide to ultrasonic thickness measurement requirements. If you want the national explanation first, start at ultrasonic testing services.

Ultrasonic weld examination with angle beams

Weld inspection is a different job from thickness gauging. A shear-wave angle-beam probe, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees, is scanned beside the weld so the sound enters the joint at an angle that suits the bevel. Before scanning, the technician builds a reference level, often a distance-amplitude correction curve, from side-drilled holes in a calibration block of the same acoustic character as the part. Indications are then compared with that reference to decide whether a reflector is a planar flaw such as lack of fusion or a crack, or a rounded one such as slag.

In San Antonio this applies to fabricated structural steel for buildings and bridges built to AWS D1.1 or D1.5, to pressure-vessel and piping repairs, and to ladder, platform and crane structure repairs at industrial plants. Where a code allows UT in place of radiography on a production weld, the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector agree the substitution before the job. See the construction code for acceptance, and see our ultrasonic testing guide for the technique overview.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

UT is the volumetric method of the conventional set: it reads through the wall, not only the surface. It finds wall loss from corrosion and erosion, laminations in plate, and internal weld flaws oriented across the sound beam. It does not replace surface methods for fine surface cracks, and its reliability falls when the surface is rough, painted thickly without removal, or when the grain structure scatters the beam, as in cast and austenitic material.

  • Couplant and contact: sound will not cross an air gap. Scaled, flaking or heavily pitted surfaces need preparation before readings mean anything.
  • Geometry: weld crowns, nozzles and tight radii limit probe positions and can hide zones from the beam.
  • Orientation: a flaw parallel to the sound beam reflects little energy, so weld scans use more than one angle and scan direction.
  • Temperature: velocity changes in hot steel, so readings on hot lines are corrected rather than accepted at face value.

When the question is a surface-breaking crack at a weld toe, the right tool is usually magnetic particle testing in San Antonio on carbon steel or penetrant testing in San Antonio on stainless and non-ferrous parts, with UT used to size or confirm.

Codes, acceptance and the Texas framework

The code that governs a job decides the procedure and the acceptance criteria. For fixed equipment, API 510 covers pressure vessels, API 570 covers piping and API 653 covers aboveground storage tanks; in each case the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis supplies the examination data, such as thickness at CMLs, for that person to evaluate. New construction and repair follow ASME Section VIII Division 1 (Appendix 12 for ultrasonic examination of welds) or ASME B31.3 (paragraph 344.6 for UT, with acceptance in Table 341.3.2). Structural steel follows AWS D1.1, including its ultrasonic provisions for groove welds, and bridge steel follows AWS D1.5. Pipeline girth welds fall under API 1104.

Texas administers its boiler law through the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation under Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code. That program covers power, heating and process steam boilers, assigns inspection intervals by the ASME code the boiler was built to, and expects inspections by TDLR or an authorized inspection agency. If your San Antonio plant has registered boilers, the UT data we collect, such as drum, header and tube-stub thickness, supports the inspector's certificate decision; it does not replace the commissioned inspector. Process safety management under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) adds the mechanical-integrity duty to inspect and test equipment under recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and pipeline operators in Texas work under the federal PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, administered for intrastate lines by the Railroad Commission of Texas.

Who does the work

Atlantis has no office in San Antonio. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which is written to ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The company was founded by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. We hold ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification for the company management system. If your plant already has a written practice and procedure, we work to those; if you do not, the Level III consulting service can write them, and see written practice development.

What the UT report contains

A usable UT record lets another Level II repeat the examination. Each report lists the component identification and drawing or tag number, the code and the procedure with its revision, the instrument, probes, wedges and calibration blocks with calibration dates, the technician and certification level, the surface condition and temperature, and the couplant used. Thickness work includes the grid or CML layout, the nominal and measured values, the minimum required wall if the owner supplies it, and a note where a reading was blocked or doubtful. Weld work includes the scan plan, the reference level, each recordable indication with location, length, amplitude and depth, and an accept or reject decision against the named criteria. Sketches mark the indications on the weld map so the repair crew can find them.

Planning a UT job in San Antonio

South Texas heat is the first planning item. Steel in direct sun in summer can run far above the temperature where standard probes and couplant behave, so we schedule shaded or early-shift work where we can, and bring high-temperature couplant for lines that are hot in service. Summer humidity is moderate, but dust and wind-blown grit on outdoor tanks and rack piping affect surface preparation, and winter mornings occasionally fall near freezing, which stiffens couplant and slows contact work. Rain stops outdoor examination because water films on the surface mask conditions.

Access matters as much as weather. Plants on the Interstate 35 and Interstate 10 corridors and the loop roads generally have badging and safety orientation; plan for that and for site-specific permits for confined space, hot work and work at height. Port San Antonio is an industrial airfield, so work near taxiways and hangar aprons follows airfield access rules set by the site operator. For outage-driven work, tell us the shutdown window and the scaffold or rope-free access plan early, so the scope is sized to what can actually be reached.

UT, MT or PT for your San Antonio job

Choose by the question. If you need remaining wall, a corrosion survey or an internal weld flaw, UT is the answer. If you need a surface or near-surface crack at a weld toe or a fillet on carbon steel, magnetic particle examination is faster and more sensitive on the surface. If the material is stainless, aluminum or any non-magnetic alloy and the concern is a surface-breaking flaw, liquid penetrant is the method. Many turnaround scopes use all three on one vessel: UT for remaining wall, MT on carbon-steel nozzle welds, PT on stainless internals. Compare them in MT versus PT or ask us to sequence them for you.

Training your own technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, our UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses follow the SNT-TC-1A recommended hours, and theory can be taken online with the UT practical simulator for hands-on practice. Hands-on practical examinations happen at the employer's facility under the employer's written practice, because under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel. See NDT training for San Antonio and check the SNT-TC-1A eligibility tool to see what experience hours a candidate needs.

faq.q: Do you have an office or lab in San Antonio?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in San Antonio. Level II technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, working under the Atlantis written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A with Level III approval of procedures and review of the reports.

faq.q: What ultrasonic services can you perform in San Antonio?
faq.a: We perform contact ultrasonic thickness testing on tanks, vessels, piping and structural steel, and angle-beam shear-wave examination of welds. We do not offer radiographic testing in the United States or any advanced ultrasonic technique.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII each contain different provisions, so the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector agree the substitution before any work begins.

faq.q: How are thickness readings kept accurate on pitted pipe?
faq.a: We use dual-element probes, calibrate on a step block of the same material, read the A-scan rather than only the digital value, and prepare the surface to bright metal where needed. Readings taken on prepared and unprepared spots are noted separately.

faq.q: Do you work on API 510, 570 or 653 equipment?
faq.a: Yes, as the examination provider. The owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and the fitness decision, and we deliver the thickness and weld data, procedures and calibration records that inspector needs to make it.

faq.q: How does Texas boiler law affect UT work at my plant?
faq.a: Texas regulates boilers through the Department of Licensing and Regulation under Health and Safety Code Chapter 755, with commissioned inspectors from the state or an insurer. Our UT data supports their decisions; it does not replace the commissioned inspection.

faq.q: How hot can the steel be for ultrasonic readings?
faq.a: Standard probes and couplant have limits, so hot lines need high-temperature probes and couplant plus a temperature correction. We confirm the surface temperature in the procedure before the job and may need the line cooled or the reading taken at a different location.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for UT in San Antonio?
faq.a: Send the component list, code, thickness range, surface condition, access notes and shutdown window through the quote form. We scope the examination, state the assumptions and reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can you train our own staff in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 UT courses follow SNT-TC-1A recommended hours, with online theory and simulator practice. Your company certifies its personnel under its written practice; Atlantis supports the training and examination records.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in San Antonio, TX
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection in San Antonio, TX: weld toes, crane hooks, tank and vessel welds, structural steel. MT to ASME and AWS. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in San Antonio, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to San Antonio plants, fabrication yards, hangars and rail sites to run magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) on carbon and low-alloy steel. We examine weld toes, lifting hardware, structural connections and pressure-equipment welds for surface and slightly subsurface cracks, and we report each finding against the acceptance criteria of your code. Describe the parts and the code through the quote request form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in San Antonio

The city's steel is varied. Automotive assembly and its supplier base use heavy press frames, fixtures, lifting beams and conveyor structure that fatigue at welds and bolted lugs. Aerospace repair and overhaul operations around the former Kelly Air Force Base need handling equipment, ground-support stands and hangar crane structure inspected for cracks at attachment welds. Energy fabricators serving South Texas build skid frames, separator vessels, lifting lugs and pipe supports, and the municipal power system has boiler casings, structural supports and rack piping.

Warehousing and logistics sites, including the railport at Port San Antonio, run overhead cranes, hoist hooks, spreader bars and forklift forks. These are the components where a fatigue crack is both likely and costly. MT is the usual method for them, since a crack at a fillet weld toe or at the root of a hook thread opens to the surface in ferromagnetic steel and shows clearly under magnetic particles. The same logic applies to tank shell-to-bottom welds at bulk storage terminals and to nozzle-to-shell welds on vessels.

How the method works, and where it stops

Magnetic particle testing magnetizes the part. A discontinuity that lies across the field lines distorts the field and leaks flux at the surface, and fine iron particles gather at the leak to form a visible line. That physics sets the limits. The part must be ferromagnetic: carbon steel and most low-alloy and martensitic steels qualify, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and titanium do not. The method finds surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities, not deep internal flaws. A crack parallel to the field gives almost no signal, which is why a second examination with the field turned roughly ninety degrees is required.

  • Surface condition: heavy scale, thick paint or weld spatter reduce sensitivity and must be removed or the procedure qualified for the coating thickness.
  • Field strength: too little field misses small cracks; too much on a sharp geometry can create false non-relevant indications.
  • Coatings and plating: a thin nonmagnetic coating may be tolerated under a qualified procedure, but this is checked with a gauge, not assumed.

When the part is stainless or non-magnetic, use penetrant testing in San Antonio. When the question is wall loss or an internal weld flaw, use ultrasonic testing in San Antonio.

Technique: yokes, prods, wet and dry particles

Most field work in San Antonio uses an electromagnetic yoke. ASME Section V, Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the technician checks this with a calibrated test weight before use. The yoke legs sit on either side of the weld, the particles are applied while the field is on, and the area is then examined for indications. After that the yoke is rotated so a second pass at roughly right angles covers cracks in any direction.

Dry powder suits rough surfaces and warm parts in dusty outdoor settings; wet visible particles suit smoother surfaces and finer cracks; wet fluorescent particles give the highest sensitivity and are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, with the light intensity and ambient white light measured against the procedure limits. Prods can pass current through a part for large casting or weld areas, though we avoid them where arc burns on the surface are unacceptable. When residual magnetism would affect later welding, machining or service, the part is demagnetized and checked with a field meter. Our magnetic particle testing guide covers the method in plain terms, and the Article 7 explainer walks through the code text.

Codes and acceptance for San Antonio work

Which criteria apply depends on what the part is. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 sets MT methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 apply to process piping. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 and bridge steel under AWS D1.5 use their own visual and magnetic particle clauses, and ASTM E709 and E1444 are the guide and practice most written procedures follow. For in-service equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector decides on repair or continued service, and Atlantis provides the crack indications and their locations and sizes.

Texas regulates boilers under Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code through the Department of Licensing and Regulation. Repairs and alterations to boilers and pressure vessels follow the National Board Inspection Code, and the commissioned inspector signs off. The MT results we supply, for example at a weld repair on a header or a lug weld, become part of that record. Process safety management in OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) expects equipment inspection under recognized good engineering practice, so cracks found by MT feed straight into your mechanical-integrity program.

Who performs the magnetic particle inspection

We have no office in San Antonio. Level II technicians mobilize to your site for the scope. They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Technical authority sits with the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification for its management system. If your procedure already exists, we follow it; if it does not, Level III consulting can produce one to your code.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

Finding a particle line is easy; deciding what it means is the skill. Relevant indications come from discontinuities such as cracks, laps and lack of fusion. Non-relevant indications come from magnetic writing, sharp section changes, the edge of a weld crown or the boundary between a weld and a heat-affected zone, where flux leaks without a flaw being present. False indications come from poor cleaning, particles trapped on rough surface or too much current. A Level II technician re-examines doubtful lines after light cleaning and re-magnetizing, and records how the call was made. A rounded indication on a hook thread and a straight line at a weld toe do not carry the same meaning, and the report says which one the technician saw.

In practice that means careful surface preparation before the yoke goes down. We remove loose scale and weld spatter with a wire brush or light grinding, keep the area free of oil, and treat painted steel according to the procedure, which sets a maximum coating thickness. Magnetic particle work on structure that has been painted and repainted for years often needs a patch cleaned to bare metal at each weld, and the owner should plan for the touch-up afterwards.

Typical San Antonio scopes

Most requests in the city fall into a handful of patterns. A plant wants periodic inspection of overhead crane hooks and runway welds as part of its rigging program. A fabricator needs final MT on structural welds before shipment to a project, to AWS D1.1 or the contract specification. A vessel repair crew needs MT on a ground-out crack repair before the weld is closed and again afterward. An operator of storage tanks wants MT on the shell-to-bottom weld or on a repaired nozzle during an internal inspection. A maintenance department wants a lifting-lug check before heavy equipment is moved. Each is sized by the number of welds or parts, the access, and the procedure, and each ends with a report your own inspector or engineer can file.

What the MT report contains

The report ties each result to its method. It names the component and its tag, the code and the procedure with revision, the equipment (yoke or bench, serial number, last lifting-power check), the particles and carrier, the field direction and number of passes, the light levels for fluorescent work, the surface condition and temperature, and the technician and level. Each indication is located on a sketch with its type, orientation and length, then marked relevant or non-relevant and accepted or rejected against the named acceptance criteria. If demagnetization was required, the residual field reading is recorded. Photographs support disputed calls without replacing the written finding.

Planning an MT job in San Antonio

Heat and dust drive local planning. In summer the surface of steel in direct sun can run well above the range at which wet particles and carriers work reliably; evaporation makes carriers dry before the pass is complete. We plan outdoor wet work for shaded or cooler periods, and we use dry powder where surface temperature rules out liquids. Wind complicates dry powder, so a screen or a shift of schedule may be required. A rare winter cold snap affects carriers less than summer heat does, but moisture on parts still ruins contrast.

For fluorescent work we need dark enough conditions; for hangar interiors and plant buildings that is often easy, while for outdoor structure a portable shroud or an after-dark window may be needed. Allow for site badging, safety orientation, and any hot work or confined space permits. Cranes and elevated structure need access equipment arranged in advance, since a yoke inspection of a hook block or runway beam is only as good as the reach. Tell us your outage dates and any access limits when you ask for the quote.

MT, PT or UT for your job in San Antonio

If the part is carbon steel and the fear is a crack at the surface, MT is typically the faster and more sensitive choice. If the part is stainless or non-ferrous, switch to penetrant. If you need to know how deep a crack runs or whether there is wall loss behind it, add ultrasonic sizing and thickness. See MT versus PT for the trade-offs, and the national page for magnetic particle testing services for scope.

Training your technicians in magnetic particle testing

For an in-house program, we offer MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses based on SNT-TC-1A recommended hours. Candidates can use NDT practice tests to check readiness, and your company certifies its own staff under its written practice. Explore San Antonio NDT training for how the courses are delivered, with the hands-on practical at your facility.

faq.q: Do you have an office in San Antonio for magnetic particle work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in San Antonio. We mobilize Level II technicians to your site for the agreed scope and bring the yokes, particles, light meters and calibration weights needed for the job.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection test?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, most low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and titanium are not magnetic and need liquid penetrant testing instead for surface-breaking flaws.

faq.q: Why does the part get examined twice?
faq.a: A crack lying parallel to the magnetic field gives almost no signal. ASME Section V Article 7 therefore calls for two examinations at roughly right angles so that cracks in any direction can be detected.

faq.q: Can you inspect crane hooks and lifting hardware?
faq.a: Yes. Hook shanks, thread roots, spreader bars, lugs and weld attachments are standard magnetic particle subjects, examined to your procedure and the rated-load program. The owner or rigging authority decides whether a cracked component returns to service.

faq.q: When do you use wet fluorescent particles?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles give the highest sensitivity and are used for fine cracks and critical welds. They need UV-A light and a darkened viewing area, and the light intensity and ambient light are checked against the procedure limits.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required?
faq.a: No. It is done when residual magnetism could interfere with service, later welding or machining, or when the specification demands it. We record the residual field reading when demagnetization is performed.

faq.q: Does Atlantis provide API inspectors for tanks and vessels?
faq.a: No. For API 510, 570 and 653 work the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record. We perform the magnetic particle examination and deliver the indication data and records that inspector requires.

faq.q: How do I request a magnetic particle inspection quote in San Antonio?
faq.a: Use the quote form to send component types, material, code, surface condition, access and your shutdown window. We scope the examination, list assumptions and reply within one business day.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in San Antonio, TX
pt.description: On-site liquid penetrant testing in San Antonio, TX: stainless piping, vessel welds, aluminum and non-magnetic parts. Visible and fluorescent PT. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in San Antonio, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to San Antonio sites for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection or PT. It is the method for surface-breaking cracks, laps and porosity on any non-porous material, including the stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys where magnetic particle testing cannot work. Tell us the parts, material and code using the quote request form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in San Antonio

Penetrant fits San Antonio's non-ferrous and stainless work. Food and beverage plants run stainless tanks, heat exchangers, jacketed vessels and sanitary piping, where weld cracks and crevice defects matter for both containment and cleanability. Aerospace repair and overhaul operations around Port San Antonio handle aluminum, titanium and nickel-alloy components and the tooling and fixtures that service them. Automotive suppliers weld aluminum and stainless brackets and exhaust components, and energy fabricators build stainless and duplex piping spools and skid-mounted equipment for South Texas operators.

Penetrant also covers carbon steel when particle testing is awkward, for instance on small bore connections, thin sections, or weld repairs where the part geometry makes yoke placement difficult. Boiler tubes and header weld repairs, valve bodies and pump casings brought in for repair, and the cladding and overlay welds on vessel internals are all routine PT subjects. Because PT depends only on a flaw being open to the surface, it suits repair shops, plant maintenance areas and field work alike.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

PT works by capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean surface, left for a dwell time so it can enter any surface-breaking discontinuity, wiped or washed off the surface, and drawn back out by a developer that makes the indication visible. The strength of the method is that it needs no special material property. The limits follow just as directly. A flaw that does not open to the surface is invisible to PT, so subsurface cracks and internal lack of fusion are missed. A crack packed with oxide, paint, grease or a previous penetrant residue cannot take up penetrant, so cleaning decides the quality of the test.

  • Porous materials: sintered, cast or rough surfaces hold penetrant everywhere and create a background that hides real flaws.
  • Prior mechanical working: grinding, shot blasting or wire brushing can smear metal across a crack mouth and close it, so cleaning by etching or controlled prep is often required.
  • Contamination of the part: on stainless and nickel alloys, penetrant materials must be low in chlorides and sulfur, which is checked on the material certificate.

For internal flaws or wall loss, add ultrasonic testing in San Antonio. For carbon-steel weld toes where speed and sensitivity matter, magnetic particle testing in San Antonio is usually the first choice.

Technique: penetrant types, removal and developer

Procedures define the penetrant type and the removal method. Type I fluorescent penetrants are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area and are chosen for fine cracks; Type II visible penetrants show red against a white developer in ordinary light and suit field work and thicker sections. Method A is water washable, Method B uses a post-emulsifier, and Method C is solvent removable, which is the usual field method because it needs only cleaner and clean lint-free wipes. ASME Section V, Article 6 and ASTM E165 are the governing practices.

The sequence is fixed. Clean and dry the surface; apply the penetrant by spray or brush and keep it wet through the dwell time given in the procedure; remove the excess carefully, since overcleaning pulls penetrant out of the flaw and undercleaning leaves a background; apply a thin, even layer of developer; allow the developing time; then examine under adequate white light or UV-A. Indications are evaluated within the time window in the procedure. Our penetrant testing simulator shows the sequence step by step, and the national penetrant testing page gives the overview.

Codes and acceptance, and the Texas context

The construction code sets acceptance. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers liquid penetrant methods and acceptance for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 covers process piping, and AWS D1.1 and D1.6 cover structural carbon steel and stainless steel structures. Where the equipment is in service under API 510 or API 570, the authorized inspector of the owner is the one who judges fitness for service; our work is to find and record the surface indications and their size and location.

Texas operates a statutory boiler program through the Department of Licensing and Regulation under Health and Safety Code Chapter 755. Inspections are performed by commissioned inspectors from the state or an authorized inspection agency, and repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. A penetrant result on a header weld repair or on a tube-to-tubesheet weld is evidence that inspector uses. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) adds the mechanical-integrity requirement for process plants covered by process safety management.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in San Antonio, so the technicians travel to your site. They work under the Atlantis written practice, written to ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians perform, interpret and document the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the technique and reviews reports. Penetrant procedures are reviewed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, who founded the company. The company management system is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. When you need a procedure that suits your penetrant lot, temperature range and surface, the Level III consulting team can write it.

Interpreting penetrant indications

A bleed-out line is not automatically a crack. Linear indications, with a length at least three times the width, usually point to cracks, laps or seams; rounded indications suggest porosity or pits; and a broad diffuse stain usually means inadequate removal. The technician evaluates each indication during the developing period, wipes and re-develops a doubtful one once if the procedure allows, and records the shape, length and position. Indications that bleed continuously from a deep crack grow quickly under developer, which is itself a clue about volume, and the report notes it. Non-relevant indications are caused by geometry, such as a weld toe notch trapping penetrant, and are documented rather than ignored.

Consistency across the job matters more than any single call. The same penetrant family, the same dwell, and the same lighting should apply to every weld in a joint population, otherwise the acceptance decision is not comparable between welds. Where fluorescent penetrant is used, the technician allows eyes to adapt in the dark area, and where visible penetrant is used, he checks the white-light level at the surface. Consumables are kept sealed, and a penetrant that has become contaminated with water or dirt is discarded and replaced rather than topped up.

Typical San Antonio penetrant scopes

The requests we see are practical. A plant wants stainless weld repairs on a process tank verified before it is returned to service. A shop wants final PT on weld joints of stainless skids and aluminum frames before shipment. An overhaul operation wants a surface check on a repaired non-ferrous fixture or a machined part. A power or process plant wants PT on socket welds and small-bore connections after a modification. A pressure-equipment repair company wants PT on a ground-out area on a vessel shell before welding and after the repair weld cools. Each scope is sized by the number of welds and surface area, the cleaning required and the access, and each ends with a report your inspector or engineer can file.

Because many San Antonio penetrant jobs are repairs, timing with the welder matters. A weld repair is examined after it has cooled to a temperature inside the procedure range, and a ground-out crack is examined before welding to show that the excavation reached sound metal. We coordinate with your welding foreman so the surface is prepared and cooled when we arrive, and we leave the area clean of developer residue, which can contaminate a later weld if it is left in the groove.

What the PT report contains

A PT report records the process so the result is reproducible. It names the component and weld, the code and procedure revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by manufacturer, family and lot number, the sensitivity level and method, the surface preparation and cleaning agents, the part and ambient temperature, the dwell and developing times, and the lighting conditions with measured light levels where required. Indications are described by shape, location, size and orientation, shown on a sketch or photograph, and labeled accepted or rejected against the named criteria. Consumable lot records are kept because several codes require material certification for sulfur and halogens on nickel and stainless parts.

Planning a penetrant job in San Antonio

Temperature is the main local variable. The standard range in ASME Section V Article 6 for the part and the penetrant materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and outside it the procedure must be qualified for the temperature in question. San Antonio summers push exposed steel past 125 degrees by mid-afternoon, which flashes off solvent cleaner and developer and dries the penetrant on the surface. For outdoor work we plan shaded or cooler periods and cool the part where necessary. Winter mornings can run cold enough to thicken penetrant, so we check the part temperature with a contact thermometer rather than estimating.

Humidity and wind affect developer drying and clean-up, and dust sticks to wet penetrant. Allow for site badging and safety orientation, for permits when the work is in a vessel or confined space, and for lighting for fluorescent work. Process areas often have restrictions on solvents near ignition sources, so the cleaning and developer products are approved before they are brought on site. Share your outage dates and the surface condition in the quote request so the preparation is scoped properly.

PT, MT or UT for your San Antonio job

Pick penetrant for non-magnetic alloys, for small or awkward geometry, and for a clear answer on whether a surface flaw is open to the surface. Pick magnetic particle for carbon steel when sensitivity and speed matter. Pick ultrasonic when the concern is below the surface. Our MT versus PT comparison sets out the differences, and the Article 6 explainer covers the code requirements in detail.

faq.q: Do you have a lab or office in San Antonio for penetrant testing?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office or lab in San Antonio. We mobilize Level II technicians to your site with the penetrant materials, light meters and thermometers required for the job.

faq.q: What can liquid penetrant testing detect?
faq.a: Only flaws that are open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams and porosity, on non-porous materials. Subsurface flaws and cracks filled with paint, oxide or grease will not show unless cleaning opens them.

faq.q: Which materials need penetrant instead of magnetic particle?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel, duplex alloys, aluminum, copper, titanium and nickel alloys are not magnetic, so penetrant is the surface method. It can also be used on carbon steel where yoke access is awkward.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, and we measure the surface temperature on the day.

faq.q: Why does surface cleaning matter so much?
faq.a: Penetrant cannot enter a crack that is blocked by oil, oxide, paint or smeared metal. Poor cleaning hides real flaws, while poor removal leaves a background that makes false indications difficult to evaluate.

faq.q: Do you test stainless steel in food processing plants?
faq.a: We examine stainless welds on tanks, vessels and piping by liquid penetrant, using materials low in halogens and sulfur and following the plant's hygiene and access rules. Findings are recorded against the applicable code or specification.

faq.q: Does Atlantis provide API authorized inspectors?
faq.a: No. For API 510, 570 and 653 equipment, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record. We perform the penetrant examination and provide documented indications and records for that inspector.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for penetrant testing in San Antonio?
faq.a: Send the component list, material, code, surface condition, access notes and outage window with the quote form. We scope the work, state our assumptions and reply within one business day.
